column4: The section pictures giving with an open hand; this ayah rejects the claim that God's hand is bound and says His hands are extended and He spends as He wills (يداه مبسوطتان ينفق كيف يشاء), a direct reversal of withholding.
Solomon asks which member of his assembly will bring the Queen's throne; this starts a concrete ask-and-transfer scene that the following ayat complete.
The jinn offers to bring the throne before Solomon rises; his spoken offer is the next step in the transfer requested in 27:38.
The throne is placed before Solomon, who calls it فضل ربي and says the gift tests gratitude; the transfer ends in the section's pattern of receiving God's favor and speaking of it.
After the throne arrives in 27:40, Solomon disguises it to test whether the Queen is guided; the passage brings the section's gift and هدى strands together in one scene.

The response recognizes the throne and says knowledge had been given before it; this completes the test begun in 27:41 and places received knowledge beside a delivered object. The speaker of the final clause is uncertain in my recollection.
Solomon asks God to forgive him and grant him a kingdom; this is the request that leads to the grant and choice over giving or holding in 38:39.
God answers Solomon's request in 38:35 by subjecting the wind to him; it names a concrete part of the kingdom later called God's عطاؤنا in 38:39.
After listing gardens, crops, and fruit, this ayah commands people to give its due on harvest day and not waste (آتوا حقه يوم حصاده ولا تسرفوا), joining provision to measured giving.

This ayah speaks of provision and God's نعمة, then asks whether people deny His favor; its picture of unequal provision and what is held back by right hands concretizes the section's hand-and-bounty link.
This rule distributes communal wealth to kin, orphans, the poor, and travelers so it will not circulate only among the rich; it gives the section's open hand a social rule against hoarding.
The next ayah identifies the poor emigrants as people expelled from homes and property who seek God's bounty; it specifies vulnerable recipients within the distribution named in 59:7.
This neighbor describes the Helpers welcoming and preferring the emigrants even while needy, and being protected from stinginess; it shows giving to the vulnerable at personal cost.
Believers are told to spend from what God has made them successors over; the section's giver-recipient handoff is framed as passing on wealth first received from God.
This ayah joins reciting God's book, prayer, and spending from His provision privately and publicly, connecting the section's spoken mention of favor to the hand that gives.
It completes the giving passage in 35:29: God pays the givers fully and increases them from His bounty, so the human gift is followed by divine return.

The ayah depicts the whole earth in God's قبضته and the heavens folded in His right hand; it gives a cosmic counterpart to the section's qahr as taking from above, while distinguishing divine sovereignty from human abuse.
Believers are told to spend from what God provided before a day with no buying, friendship, or intercession; it makes present giving a response to provision before the Hereafter's reckoning.

This ayah names the recipients of obligatory charity, including the poor, needy, debtors, and stranded traveler; it supplies a concrete distribution setting for the section's asker and vulnerable recipients.
It pairs men and women who give charity with those who lend God a goodly loan, promising multiplication and a noble reward; the section's handoff is explicitly answered by God's return.
The command to spend for one's own good is paired with protection from شح (stinginess); it makes the closed hand a spiritual danger, as in the section's contrast between giving and withholding.

After the feeding and pure intention in 76:8–9, God protects the givers from that day's evil and gives them radiance and joy; this completes the passage with a return that answers the section's promised satisfaction.

The section connects هدى with a gift; this ayah says God guides those who seek His pleasure by the Book from darkness to light and to paths of peace, making guidance a received benefit with a destination.
The ayah says God's hand is above the believers' hands as they pledge allegiance; this is a covenantal hand relation rather than a material transfer, but it places human hands under divine authority.
